nodes.title: Piece Rate (Lazear 2000, Safelite)
nodes.content:
**The reference contract**

Pay per unit of output. Safelite auto-glass workers switched from hourly to per-windshield → **+44%** productivity (Lazear 2000). About half of the gain is *effort* (moral hazard resolved), half is *sorting* (high-productivity workers self-select in).

**Signal**: individual measured output.

**Model context**
- Firm output: $V(F) = g(\text{effort}) + \varepsilon$
- Worker utility: $U(W) = c(\text{income}) - h(\text{effort})$
- Piece rate connects the two by tying income directly to $g(\text{effort})$.

**Six failure modes** (see failure snippets below):
1. Imperfect measurement → risk transfer
2. Multitasking distortion
3. Ratchet effect
4. Risk transfer to worker
5. Cooperation collapse
6. Goodhart / bunching at thresholds

**Safelite preconditions** (see Conditions snippet): perfect measurability, clear quality standard, individual production.

nodes.title: Failure 1: Imperfect Performance Measurement
nodes.content:
**Problem**

The signal we contract on is $s = g(\text{effort}) + \varepsilon$, not effort itself. Any noise $\varepsilon$ in the measurement gets transmitted into the worker's pay.

**Consequences**
- Risk-averse workers demand a wage premium for bearing this noise → higher wage bill.
- Or the firm dampens the piece rate to reduce risk exposure → weaker incentive → less effort.
- Either way, first-best not achievable (Holmström–Milgrom 1987 optimal linear contract trades off risk and incentive intensity).

**Fixes** → see solutions

nodes.title: Failure 2: Multitasking (Holmström–Milgrom 1991)
nodes.content:
**Problem**

If you reward one task among several, workers crowd out the un-rewarded tasks.

**Evidence**
- Asch (1990), Larkin (2014): piece rates on tasks A, B, C → worker picks only the mispriced (arbitrage) one.
- If firm tracks 3 tasks, worker will find the highest-marginal-return one and dump the rest.

**Why it happens**
Worker's cost of effort is convex; marginal reward differs across tasks. Optimal worker response is corner solution unless the firm can equalize marginal incentives across ALL relevant dimensions.

**Fixes** → see solutions

nodes.title: Failure 3: Ratchet Effect (Gibbons 1987)
nodes.content:
**Problem**

Worker exerts low effort in easy periods so the firm doesn't discover the task is easy and raise the quota next period. Roy (1952); Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005).

**Mechanism**
Worker's optimal effort today depends on how effort maps to *tomorrow's target*, not just today's pay. If high output → tighter quota tomorrow, then output must be dampened.

**Fix — Holmström (1982); Shleifer (1985)**: quota indexed to *peers*, not own history — own effort no longer feeds own standard. Yardstick competition.

**Fixes** → see solutions

nodes.title: Failure 4: Risk Transfer to Worker
nodes.content:
**Problem**

Pay = f(output), and output varies for reasons the worker cannot control: machine downtime, random customer arrivals, seasonal variation, task-difficulty heterogeneity.

**Consequence**
Risk-averse workers dislike income variance; they demand a risk premium. Firm pays MORE in expected wage bill just to get the same expected effort. The insurance-vs-incentive tradeoff (Holmström–Milgrom 1987) is the core of contract theory.

**Fixes** → see solutions.

**Note**: Team pay (S4) and Ownership (S8) make this WORSE — they load systematic firm-level risk.

nodes.title: Failure 5: Cooperation Collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003)
nodes.content:
**Evidence**
Garment plant switched from team pay to individual piece rates → total output FELL despite rising individual effort. Workers stopped teaching, helping, covering. Also Encinosa–Gaynor–Rebitzer (2007) on physician groups.

**Mechanism**
Under piece rates, time spent helping a peer = zero personal reward + opportunity cost of your own output. Rational response: withdraw from cooperation. Knowledge transfer disappears.

**Fixes** → see solutions.

**Note**: Tournaments (S2) make this WORSE — helping a peer directly lowers your relative rank.

nodes.title: Failure 6: Goodhart / Bunching
nodes.content:
**Evidence**
- Oyer (1998): salespeople bunch deals before fiscal year-end.
- Larkin (2014): software sales *sandbag* large deals to avoid ratcheting next quarter.
- Camerer–Farber–Falk: taxi drivers, bike messengers stop at daily income target (backward-bending supply from loss aversion).

**Mechanism**
Any quota threshold creates a kink where marginal piece rate drops to zero (or turns negative via ratchet). Workers bunch AT the threshold — never above.

'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.'

**Fixes** → see solutions

nodes.title: Safelite Preconditions (when piece rates DO work)
nodes.content:
**Three conditions that made Safelite work**

1. **Output perfectly measurable**: install-a-windshield-or-not; discrete, countable, homogeneous.
2. **Quality standard clear**: any leak / failure → worker returns to fix, unpaid, on own time. Solves the quality-quantity multitasking problem via ex-post penalty.
3. **Production individual**: no cooperation externalities to destroy. One worker, one car, one windshield. No mentoring, no joint production, no knowledge spillovers.

**Implication for us**
Quindi's setting almost certainly violates #3 (cooperation matters) and possibly #1 (AI-assisted output is multi-dimensional). The evaluation index must **price cooperation** and cannot rely on a single scalar throughput measure.

nodes.title: S2. Tournament / Rank-Order Contest (Lazear–Rosen 1981)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: your *rank* among peers, not your level.

**Solves**
- Cancels common shocks (market, weather, task difficulty) via relative comparison — filters $\varepsilon$ if it hits everyone.
- Simple prize structure; only ordinal ranking needed, not cardinal output.
- Fights the ratchet: workers can't hide capacity if effort still moves rank.

**Breaks**
- **Sabotage** (Chan 1996; Dye 1984; Lazear 1989): hurting a peer raises your rank as much as improving yourself.
- **Collusion**: everyone agrees to low effort.
- **Kills cooperation completely** — helping a peer is directly costly.
- Discourages risky innovation late in the round if you're ahead.

**Use when**: individual output measurable up to a common shock, peer group homogeneous, cooperation not required.

nodes.title: S3. Fixed Wage + Efficiency Wage (Shapiro–Stiglitz 1984)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: none directly — pay is flat. Motivation comes from *threat of dismissal* under monitoring, plus a wage above market-clearing so the job is worth keeping.

**Solves**
- Removes all output-based risk from worker (attractive to risk-averse workers).
- Handles jobs where output is unmeasurable or quality dominates quantity.
- No multitasking distortion — worker isn't paid on any specific task.

**Breaks**
- Requires **credible monitoring** AND **credible dismissal** — if firing is costly (regulation, union), incentive collapses.
- Involuntary unemployment as equilibrium feature.
- No high-powered incentive → productivity ceiling.

**Use when**: output signals are noisy or gameable; quality > quantity; firm has monitoring infrastructure.

nodes.title: S4. Team Pay / Profit Sharing (Kandel–Lazear 1992; Weitzman–Kruse 1990)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: group-level output — team quota, plant profits, firm profit.

**Solves**
- Rewards cooperation, mentoring, mutual help directly.
- Aligns worker to firm value (profit sharing = residual claim).
- Peer pressure polices free-riders in *small* teams (Kandel–Lazear).

**Breaks**
- **Free-rider problem grows with N**: marginal reward on own effort is $\approx 1/N$.
- Requires observability *between* peers so social pressure operates.
- Loads systematic risk (firm-wide shocks) onto workers — worsens Failure 4.

**Use when**: small tight teams with strong cooperation externalities and mutual observability (surgical team, small startup).

nodes.title: S5. Deferred Compensation / Seniority Pay (Lazear 1979, 1981)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: tenure. Pay < marginal product early, > marginal product late.

**Solves**
- Bonds worker to firm — being fired for shirking forfeits back-loaded pay.
- Solves moral hazard when short-run output isn't measurable but reputation shapes retention.
- Reduces turnover; captures returns to firm-specific investment.

**Breaks**
- Requires **credible commitment** from firm not to fire senior workers arbitrarily.
- Creates incentives for mandatory retirement (Lazear 1979 predicts this).
- Weakens mobility — inefficient if outside options shift.

**Use when**: firm-specific human capital matters, output hard to measure period-by-period, firm has commitment technology (large stable firms).

nodes.title: S6. Career Concerns / Implicit Incentives (Fama 1980; Holmström 1982)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: your *future outside wage*, priced by the labor market from your observed output.

**Solves**
- Motivates effort without an explicit contract — good today = better wage tomorrow at other firms.
- Works when firm can't credibly commit but the labor market can.
- Naturally captures multidimensional output — market cares about overall ability.

**Breaks**
- **Horizon effect**: incentive weakens toward retirement (Gibbons–Murphy 1992).
- Effort tilted toward visible, market-legible activities → private-value tasks under-provided.
- Requires market observability of individual output.

**Use when**: high-visibility labor markets (CEOs, academics, professional services).

nodes.title: S7. Subjective Evaluation + Bonus (MacLeod 2003; Baker–Gibbons–Murphy 1994)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: manager's private assessment, converted to bonus/promotion.

**Solves**
- Handles multitasking, quality, hard-to-quantify contributions.
- Manager can down-weight lucky outcomes and reward true effort.
- Preserves flexibility to reward cooperation, culture, mentoring.

**Breaks**
- **Influence activities** (Milgrom 1988): workers persuade the manager instead of producing.
- Favoritism, discrimination, arbitrary variation.
- Requires a **relational contract**: manager must credibly commit to fair evaluation (MacLeod 2003). Reneging destroys the equilibrium.
- Legally hard to defend if evaluations diverge from measurables.

**Use when**: output is complex, multi-dimensional, hard to game via explicit metrics; long employment relationships with repeated interaction.

nodes.title: S8. Ownership / Equity (Hansmann 1996; Kruse–Blasi 1997)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: firm value — worker holds a residual claim (stock, options, partnership share, ESOP).

**Solves**
- Aligns effort with long-run firm value → solves multitasking + horizon jointly.
- Signals commitment; attracts high-type workers.
- No need for explicit performance metrics.

**Breaks**
- Free-rider grows with $N$ (each worker owns $\approx 1/N$).
- Loads undiversified risk onto workers (labor income *and* wealth co-move).
- Governance costs — worker-owners may block value-creating layoffs.
- Requires liquidity / vesting to prevent early cash-out.

**Use when**: small firm, high-skill workers, long horizon, output primarily reflects team effort (early-stage startup, law/consulting partnership).

nodes.title: S9. Selection-Based Pay Structure (Lazear 1986, 2000)
nodes.content:
**Signal**: the *contract itself* acts as a filter — the pay structure attracts one type and repels another.

**Solves**
- You don't need to motivate ex-post; you need to attract the right type ex-ante.
- Lazear (2000): $\approx$ **half** of the Safelite 44% productivity gain was *sorting*, not effort — high-productivity workers self-select into piece-rate firms.
- Reduces monitoring cost — the contract does the screening.

**Breaks**
- Requires labor-market heterogeneity and mobility.
- Sorting alone is often insufficient; usually combined with incentives.
- Can create adverse selection if the signal the contract offers is misread.

**Use when**: heterogeneous labor market, you can't observe type directly, you want a self-enforcing filter.
